extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics; artists, poets, critics, and philosophers interested in theories of beauty and the sublime
extracted.subtask_description: A concise set of aesthetic principles describing what qualities produce the feelings of beauty and of the sublime in objects (visual, tactile, auditory, etc.), with causal commentary on how pain, fear, and association contribute to the sublime. Useful for evaluating or producing artworks, descriptions, or designs that aim to evoke beauty or the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparatively small
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty, as a merely sensible quality, is to be comparatively small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that love tends to attach to small, pleasing things while admiration (sublime) dwells on great and terrible objects. Large objects are more likely to produce the sublime; smallness is a recurrent condition of beauty. Example/contrast: we call little birds and smaller beasts endearing; 'a great beautiful thing' is scarcely ever used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness: a quality so essential to beauty that the author cannot recall anything beautiful that is not smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smooth leaves, smooth garden slopes, smooth streams, smooth coats, smooth skins, and polished surfaces contribute greatly to beauty. Any ruggedness, sudden projection, or sharp angle is highly contrary to the idea of beauty. If a beautiful object is given a broken or rugged surface, it ceases to please; conversely, lacking many other constituents, if it retains smoothness it can become more pleasing than many others without it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual variation (variety without angularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of beautiful bodies never continue long in the same right line; they vary direction insensibly and change under the eye by a deviation continually carrying on without obvious beginning or end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the dove and by the neck/breasts of a woman: surfaces are 'melted into one another', presenting continuous change but no sudden protuberance. Anti-pattern: angular figures and sudden broken variation (sharp changes) are not found in truly beautiful natural objects and are judged ugly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy (appearance of fragility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appearance of delicacy, and even of fragility, is almost essential to beauty; an air of robustness and strength is prejudicial to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: delicate myrtle, orange, jasmine, vine, and flowery species are viewed as vegetable beauties rather than robust forest trees (oak, ash). Among animals, delicacy (greyhound, Arabian horse) is more amiable than brute strength. In humans, timidity and delicacy in women enhance beauty. Caveat: weakness due to bad health is not beauty because it alters other conditions (colour, form) and causes collapse, wrinkles, and right lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour: cleanness and mildness
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours of beautiful bodies must not be dusky or muddy but clean and fair; they should not be of the strongest kind — milder colours are more appropriated to beauty (light greens, soft blues, weak whites, pink reds, violets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong or vivid colours, if present, are usually diversified so that no single glaring colour dominates. In fine complexions colours are mixed with gradations that make boundaries impossible to fix; dubious/iridescent colours (peacock necks, drake heads) are agreeable. Colour and shape work closely together to produce beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversification of strong colours
rubrics_metrics.description: If colours are strong and vivid, they are agreeable only when diversified; variety tempers the glare of each colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variegated flowers and mixed complexions show how diversification reduces the intensity of each colour and increases beauty. Anti-pattern: a uniform strong glaring colour is less beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy: expression of amiable mind qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The face (physiognomy) contributes considerably to beauty, especially in humans: the face should be expressive of gentle and amiable qualities that correspond with softness, smoothness, and delicacy of outward form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners give a determination to the countenance; to form a finished human beauty the face must join agreeable qualities of mind to those of the body. Physiognomy can join the effects of agreeable mind-qualities to physical beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: The eye: clearness, motion, and harmonious union
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauty of the eye consists first in its clearness (the 'water' not being dull or muddy); secondly in its motion (slow and languid motion more beautiful than brisk); thirdly in its harmonious union with neighbouring parts (no strong deviation or exact geometrical figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearness attracts like transparent substances (diamonds, clear water). Motion contributes by continually shifting direction but should be gentle. The eye's principal power often arises from being expressive of qualities of mind (physiognomy). Anti-pattern: eyes with dull/muddy water, brisk/aggressive motion, or strong geometric separation from surrounding features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ugliness (as opposite to beauty but not to fitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ugliness is, in all respects, the opposite of the qualities laid down for beauty, but it is not necessarily the opposite of proportion and fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thing can be very ugly and yet have perfect proportions or fit its uses. Ugliness can also be consistent with an idea of the sublime when united with qualities that excite strong terror. This highlights that beauty and ugliness are distinct from mere fitness or functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gracefulness (posture and motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gracefulness, closely related to beauty, pertains to posture and motion and requires no appearance of difficulty, a small inflection of the body, and composure of parts not encumbering each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace consists in ease, roundness, and delicacy of attitude and motion — the 'je ne sais quoi' observed in statues like the Venus de Medicis or the Antinous. Anti-pattern: movements showing difficulty, sharp and sudden angles, or encumbered parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and speciousness (regular polished composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An object composed of smooth and polished parts, not pressing upon each other and showing some regular shape, is elegant; when such qualities occur on a large scale the object is fine or specious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance differs from the beautiful by its regularity; it applies especially to delicate and regular works of art that imitate no determinate object in nature (e.g., elegant buildings and pieces of furniture). Large dimensions combined with these qualities move the effect away from 'mere beauty' toward 'fine' or 'specious'.

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful in feeling (touch): slight resistance, softness, and continuous gentle variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies pleasant to the touch are so by slightness of resistance to motion along the surface (smooth) or pressure of parts on one another (soft); a combination of both yields chief pleasure of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure from touch is increased when the surface continually varies but never suddenly; angular and sudden changes (sharp edges) are disagreeable to touch. Examples: soft, smooth, variegated, unangular bodies elicit touching pleasure analogous to sight. The touch also has distinct pleasures (softness, moderate warmth) not shared by sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sudden tactile/thermal applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden application or abrupt change (even if not violent) is disagreeable to feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a finger suddenly warmer or colder makes one start; a slight unexpected tap is disagreeable. This supports the broader rule that sudden changes in surface direction or sensation reduce beauty; thus gradualness is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy of pleasures across senses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong correspondence between what pleases different senses; qualities that cause pleasure in one sense often have analogous causes in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that color dispositions that are beautiful to the eye would, if perceivable by touch, be grateful to the touch; similarly, sweet metaphors apply across senses. This principle helps form a unified idea of beauty across sight, touch, hearing, taste, and smell.

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful in sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful sounds are soft and delicate; the beauty in music agrees with softness, winding continuity, unbroken continuance, and easy gradation rather than loudness or stark contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beautiful music will not bear loudness, strength, shrillness, harshness, or excessive depth; it favors clear, even, smooth, weak notes. Great variety and quick transitions often excite mirth or tumultuous passions and are contrary to the languor/melancholic character of the beautiful. Example: Milton's 'linked sweetness long drawn out' as an apt description of musical beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and smell analogous to other senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste and smell adhere to the same general dispositions as sight, touch, and hearing in what is agreeable or beautiful, though their specific qualities may be less obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphors (e.g., 'sweetness') are used across senses; where taste and smell are obscure we can refer to the common efficient cause of beauty across senses. Use cross-sensory comparison to clarify ambiguous cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between the sublime and the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime and the beautiful are fundamentally contrasted: sublime objects are vast, rugged, and often dark/gloomy and massive; beautiful objects are relatively small, smooth, light, delicate, and avoid strong deviations from graceful lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two are founded on different affects (sublime on pain/fear, beauty on pleasure). When an object is intended to affect the mind by a predominant property, consistency among the object's other qualities strengthens that effect. Examples of contrasts: beauty shuns the right line and loves insensible deviation; the great (sublime) sometimes loves the right line and strong deviations; beauty is light and delicate, the great is solid and massive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient cause — association
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the occasions of our passions are given and governed by associations formed early in life, making it hard to distinguish natural effects from associative ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that while association explains many responses (antipathies, fears), it would be absurd to ascribe all effects to association; some things must be originally agreeable or disagreeable. Therefore, when explaining causes of beauty or sublimity, first examine natural properties before invoking association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient cause — pain and fear as foundation of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is qualified to cause terror is a foundation for the sublime; pain and fear produce the same bodily effects and thus underlie the emotion of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke describes bodily signs of violent pain and fear (teeth set, contracted eyebrows, wrinkled forehead, rolled eyes, hair standing on end, shrieks) and argues that pain and terror act on the same bodily parts producing tension or convulsion of the nerves. Because bodily dispositions can induce corresponding passions in the mind, objects that suggest danger or pain can produce the sublime. This is both descriptive (symptoms) and prescriptive (to evoke the sublime, suggest terror or danger, or produce similar bodily dispositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily disposition and mimicry influence feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting the gestures, looks, or bodily posture of a passion can turn the mind to that passion; bodily disposition is intimately connected to mental states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Campanella mimicked faces and gestures to enter dispositions of others; the author notes mimicking angry or frightened gestures can involuntarily induce the matching passion. Likewise, opiates or stimulants can suspend or induce passions by altering bodily disposition. Practical implication: to produce or inhibit certain passions, alter bodily posture/gesture or the body's disposition.
